entries.definition: Digital Mobile Radio, the ETSI digital radio standard (TS 102 361).
Time division multiple access. A DMR channel carries two conversations by alternating them in 30 ms slots.
One of the two time slots of a DMR channel, TS1 and TS2.
A number from 0 to 15 a DMR channel uses. Radios only hear calls with their color code.
One DMR transmission in a slot: 264 bits, with a sync pattern or embedded signaling in the middle.
The 48-bit pattern in the middle of a burst. It tells the receiver the burst's kind (voice or data, base station or radio) and its timing.
Common announcement channel: 24 bits ahead of each burst a repeater sends. It carries the slot number and short link control.
Link control: the call's addressing (source, destination, group or private) that DMR repeats through a voice call.
Control signaling block: a one-burst DMR message for signaling such as call alert, radio check and Tier III control.
Multi block control: a DMR signaling message that spans several bursts.
Service access point: the field in a DMR data header that says what the payload is (IP, short data, GPS and so on).
Source port ID: the index in a compressed UDP/IP header that stands for a well-known UDP port.
Protocol data unit: one packet or message of a protocol, as the standard defines its fields.
Full link control opcode: the field of a link control message that says its kind.
A DMR group number. Everyone listening to it hears calls to it.
A DMR call to one radio.
DMR talkgroup 16777215, heard by every radio on the slot.
A DMR page that makes another radio ring.
A DMR request another radio answers automatically, to show it is on and in range.
DMR packet data the receiving radio acknowledges. What didn't arrive is sent again.
A short text, usually a callsign and name, sent along with DMR voice.
A DMR header that announces encryption with a changing key. RadioFoundry never plays such calls.
How long after a call a repeater or radio keeps the call's talkgroup ready for a reply.
DMR radio to radio on one frequency, with no repeater. The standard calls it DMO.
DMR through a repeater, which receives on one frequency and transmits on another. The standard calls it RMO.
The conventional DMR tier of the standard (TS 102 361-2): repeaters and direct mode without trunking.
The trunked DMR tier of the standard (TS 102 361-4): a control channel assigns traffic channels.
Trunked station control channel: the Tier III channel that carries control signaling.
Air interface specification, the ETSI name for DMR's over-the-air rules.
The Tier III CSBK a trunked base station sends to announce the system and its slot timing.
Link control start/stop: the 2-bit field of a burst's embedded signaling that says which fragment it carries.
Base station: the repeater or modem side of a DMR link, as opposed to the radio (MS).
Bit error rate: the share of received bits that were wrong. A measure of how clean a signal is.
DVSI's voice codec used by DMR. Not part of RadioFoundry. Taken from each radio's stock firmware.
A voice codec. DMR uses AMBE+2.
Frequency modulation: the analog voice mode. Speech moves the carrier's frequency.
How far an FM transmitter's frequency swings from the channel center. It sets loudness and bandwidth.
The width of an FM channel: 12.5 kHz (narrow) or 25 kHz (wide).
Continuous tone coded squelch system: a sub-audible tone on FM that opens the squelch only for the right signal.
Digital coded squelch: a sub-audible digital code on FM that opens the squelch only for the right signal.
The level a received signal must exceed before the radio plays it.
Received signal strength indicator: how strong the received signal is, in dBm.
Parts per million: a frequency error as a fraction of the frequency. At 450 MHz, 1 ppm is 450 Hz.
Transmitting on one frequency and receiving on another at the same time. Repeaters do, and so does the duplex hotspot setup.

Single frequency repeater. It repeats a call from one timeslot on the other timeslot of the same frequency. In MMDVM SFR the hotspot repeats, turned on by its host. In standalone SFR a channel repeats on its own (not built yet).
Phase locked loop: the circuit that holds the radio's synthesizer on its frequency.
The part that makes the radio's transmit and receive frequencies.
Power amplifier: the stage that boosts the transmit signal to the output power.
Voltage controlled oscillator: the oscillator in a synthesizer, tuned by a voltage.
Variable frequency oscillator: tuning any frequency by hand instead of a stored channel.
Voice-operated transmit.
Transmit timeout: the longest transmission the radio allows.
Listening on two channels, A and B, and talking on the selected one. With one receiver the radio alternates between them.
Serial peripheral interface: the 4-wire bus the processor uses to talk to chips such as the modem.
Inter-integrated circuit: a 2-wire bus for small chips such as the RF transceiver.
Device Firmware Upgrade: the USB protocol of the radio's bootloader.
Microcontroller: the processor that runs the firmware.
Digital signal processor: a chip, or a processor core, that does the audio and modem math.
Universal Serial Bus. The radio uses it for the debug link, the network mode and firmware updates.
Global positioning system: the satellite receiver that gives the radio its position.
The HRC6000 family: the baseband chip that codes and decodes DMR bursts. The radios that use it are in the radio survey.
The HRC7000 family: the baseband chip of the C-SKY class radios. The radios that use it are in the radio survey.
The RF transceiver chip that sets the frequency, deviation and power of many handheld DMR radios. Programmed over I2C.
Motorola's DMR product line. Its extensions (ARS, TMS, LRRP, Capacity Plus) are not in the ETSI standard.
A MOTOTRBO single-site trunking mode in which the radios share a pool of repeater channels.
A MOTOTRBO multi-site trunking system with a central controller.
A MOTOTRBO system of several Capacity Plus sites joined by a network.
Automatic Registration Service: a radio tells a presence server it is on the air.
Text message service: Motorola's text message format on DMR. The standard's own short data uses other formats.
Location Request and Response Protocol: a dispatcher asks a radio for its position. Motorola's position format; the standard has LIP.
A fixed voice scrambling from Motorola and Anytone radios. Not encryption.
Customer programming software: the program that writes the codeplug. RadioFoundry uses qdmr.
Common air interface: Motorola's name for the DMR air interface, also the name of its IP addressing on the air.
A radio a dispatch program on a computer uses to reach the fleet over the air.
The number that identifies your radio on DMR. Amateur IDs come from RadioID.net.
A worldwide amateur DMR network of linked servers and talkgroups.
A small DMR modem that connects radios nearby to a DMR network over the internet.
Automatic Packet Reporting System: positions and short messages shared between amateur stations.
A station that passes APRS packets between the air and the APRS-IS internet network.
A simple protocol between a computer's APRS program and a radio modem (TNC).
Terminal node controller: the modem that turns packet data into audio tones and back.
Audio frequency shift keying: data as two audio tones on an FM carrier. APRS at 1200 baud uses it.
Multi-Mode Digital Voice Modem: the modem protocol MMDVMHost speaks.
Hamlib's network rig control protocol, used by loggers and SDR programs.
Multicast DNS: finding a device on a local network by a `.local` name.
Simple Network Management Protocol: reading a device's state over the network.
Trivial File Transfer Protocol: a minimal way to copy files to and from a device.
Network control model: the USB class that makes the radio appear as a network adapter.
Point-to-point protocol: IP over a serial link.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: how a device gets its IP address on a network.
The radio's programming: channels, zones, contacts, talkgroup lists, DMR ID.
A free, open source codeplug editor for DMR radios.
A named list of channels.
A person in the codeplug: name and DMR ID.
The talkgroups a channel listens to. The codeplug calls it the RX group list.
Where PTT goes: a talkgroup, a person or all call.
A talk target used for one call and its reply window.
The time after a call during which PTT answers it.
A change that lasts until the channel changes or you press Back on Home. Hold OK to keep it.
Opening the squelch (FM) or hearing all talkgroups (DMR) while a key is held.
Playing every talkgroup on the timeslot (promiscuous mode; "hear all" in older RadioFoundry builds).
RadioFoundry's list of stations heard and calls made.
Push to talk: the key that transmits.
Hardware in the loop: tests that run against a real radio, and a bench radio or SDR for the other side.
Software in the loop: tests that run the firmware's core on the host with a simulated radio.
Software defined radio: a receiver that digitizes the radio spectrum so software can decode it. The SDR bench uses one.
RadioFoundry's USB serial protocol for reading state and driving the radio from a computer.
A small program that runs on the radio in place of the firmware so the computer can read or write flash without the stock bootloader.
The code and description of one radio model's hardware wiring: pins, chips, memory map.
Hardware abstraction layer: the interfaces the core uses instead of touching a chip.
System on chip: the processor and its on-chip peripherals.
A CONFIG_ option that turns a feature's code in or out of the build.
The firmware a radio shipped with, before RadioFoundry. Each RadioFoundry radio takes its voice codec from it.
Receive.
Transmit.
Radio frequency: the signal in the air, as opposed to audio or data inside the radio.
European Telecommunications Standards Institute, which publishes the DMR standard.
Very high frequency: 30 to 300 MHz. The amateur 2 m band is VHF.
Ultra high frequency: 300 MHz to 3 GHz. The amateur 70 cm band is UHF.
Dual tone multi frequency: the touch tones a keypad sends, in the audio.
Cyclic redundancy check: a checksum that detects damaged data.
Forward error correction: extra bits that let the receiver repair errors without a resend.
Error correcting code: a code that repairs damaged bits, such as the one a NAND flash needs.
Universal asynchronous receiver transmitter: a serial port.
Analog to digital converter.
Digital to analog converter.
Pulse code modulation: audio as a stream of sample numbers.
Inter-IC sound: the bus audio samples travel on between chips.
Direct memory access: moving data between memory and a peripheral without the processor.
General purpose input/output: a pin the firmware can read or drive.
Pulse width modulation: a pin switched on and off to give an average level, as for backlight or tone.
Real-time operating system: the scheduler that runs the firmware's tasks.
First in, first out: a queue of data between a producer and a consumer.
The flash chip type that holds large data, such as the codeplug and contacts, in some radios.
The flash chip type that holds code and can run it in place.
Electrically erasable programmable read-only memory: a small chip that keeps settings.
Static RAM: the processor's fast working memory.
Random access memory: working memory that loses its content at power off.
Read-only memory: code fixed in the chip.
User Datagram Protocol: IP packets with no delivery guarantee.
Transmission Control Protocol: IP connections with ordered, guaranteed delivery.
Internet Protocol: the addressing and packet layer of networks.
The text format GPS receivers use to report position and time.
Short message service: text messages. On DMR, short data carries them.
A text file format. qdmr stores its codeplug as YAML.
Comma separated values: a table as plain text, as programming software exports it.
User interface: the screen, keys and menus.
Light-emitting diode: the radio's status light.
A Chinese maker of DMR radios.
Unified data transport: DMR short data sent as a plain block of bytes.
Block product turbo code: the error correction on DMR headers and control blocks.
Embedded signaling: the 32 bits in the middle of a voice burst that carry link control.
Feature set ID: the byte that says whether a message is standard or manufacturer specific.
Temperature compensated crystal oscillator: the stable clock the radio's frequency is derived from.
Automatic gain control: the receiver adjusting itself to the signal level.
Automatic frequency control: following a transmitter that is slightly off frequency.
Frequency shift keying: data as frequency steps. DMR uses 4-level FSK.
Amplitude modulation: speech varies the carrier's strength. Airband uses it.
Signal to noise ratio.
The UDP stream that carries a call's audio between RadioFoundry and a network gateway.
USB On-The-Go: the controller can act as the host or the device.
Serial wire debug: the two-wire debug port of ARM processors.
A debug and test port of many processors.
Link-time optimization: the compiler optimizes across files. It shrinks the firmware.
Execute in place: running code straight from flash.
Central processing unit.
Liquid crystal display: the radio's screen.
Personal computer.
Acknowledgment: the reply that says a message arrived.
Most significant bit (or byte): the first, highest-value one.
Binary coded decimal: each decimal digit in 4 bits.
The 7-bit character set of plain text.
Exclusive or: a bit operation that flips bits where the other operand has a 1.
Kilobytes (1024 bytes).
Operating system.
Continuous integration: the checks every change must pass (tools/ci.sh).
GNU General Public License. RadioFoundry does not use GPL code.
The permissive license RadioFoundry uses.
RadioFoundry, this firmware.
Identifier: a number or name that picks out one thing.
The key that selects or confirms.
STMicroelectronics, the maker of the STM32 processors.
STMicroelectronics' family of ARM microcontrollers. The radios that use it are in the radio survey.
Secure Digital: removable memory card.
Mobile station: the radio, as opposed to the base station (BS).
Message indicator: the value that changes with each call and keys its encryption. It travels in the PI header.
Reverse channel: signaling the receiver sends back to the transmitter during a call, in space the burst leaves free.
The 7 bits at the start of a CACH: AT, TC, LCSS and Hamming parity.
Access type: the TACT bit that tells a radio whether the slot is free to transmit in.
TDMA channel: the TACT bit that names the timeslot, so a radio can tell TS1 from TS2.
Data type: the field of a burst's slot type that says what the burst carries (header, terminator, rate 1/2 block and so on).
Defined data format: the field of a short data header that says how its payload is coded (7-bit text, ISO 8859, UTF-16 and so on).
Last block: the flag that marks the final block of a CSBK or data message.
Protect flag: the bit in link control that marks a protected (encrypted) call.
Fragment sequence number: counts the fragments of a data packet that was split.
Short link control opcode: the field of a short LC message that says its kind.
CSBK opcode: the field of a CSBK that says its kind.
Data packet format: the field of a data header that says what follows (unconfirmed or confirmed data, UDT, short data).
Logical link ID: the 24-bit address (a DMR ID or a talkgroup number) in a data header.
Source address ID: the field of a compressed UDP/IP header that says where the source IP address comes from, for example from the LLID.
Logical physical channel number: the number of a channel in a Tier III channel plan.
TSCC alternate slot: a second control slot of a Tier III site.
The controller of a Tier III system: the infrastructure side the radio talks to.
The analog trunking standard that Tier III descends from.
Dynamic group number assignment: the Tier III system moves a radio into a talkgroup over the air.
Ambient listening service: a dispatcher turns on a radio's microphone remotely.
Public switched telephone network. Tier III can connect calls to it.
Private automatic branch exchange: an office telephone system. Tier III can connect calls to it.
Off air call set up: signaling that sets up a call before voice is sent. The radio asks over the air and waits for the answer.
Full off air call set up: OACSU with alerting, so the called radio rings and answers before voice.
DMR location area: how many of the most significant bits of SITE form SYS_AREA, the registration area.
A 3-octet number XORed into the Tier III authentication response when a network uses it.
The 16-bit system code of a Tier III system: MODEL, NET, SITE and PAR. C_ALOHA carries all of it, the CACH the top 14 bits.
The Tier III system parameters a TSCC sends in its CACH (SLCO 0010): model, network, site, registration flag and slot counter.
The same system parameters a Tier III payload channel sends in its CACH (SLCO 0011).
A Tier III CSBK that checks on a radio: an authentication challenge or the called party's radio check.
A Tier III CSBK in which a radio acknowledges or answers, for example the authentication response.
The Tier III CSBK a radio sends to ask for something on the control channel: registration, a call.
A Tier III CSBK in which the TSCC accepts a request.
A Tier III grant: the TSCC tells radios which payload channel carries a call. PV is a private voice call, TV a talkgroup voice call, BTV a broadcast talkgroup voice call.
The CSBK that tells a repeater to start transmitting. It wakes a repeater.
Motorola's style of single frequency repeater, with different inbound and outbound color codes.
Dual Capacity Direct Mode: Motorola's direct mode that carries two calls on one frequency, one per timeslot.
IP Site Connect: Motorola's linking of repeaters over IP.
A Motorola radio control protocol; XCMP commands travel over it. Neither is part of the standard.
Automatic number identification: the caller's ID sent as tones in an analog call.
